findings.issue: The text says node denominators divide Gamma_X 2^alpha with alpha = J + O(I) + mu K_mu, 'so they do not grow with the number of stages'. Read literally this is false: alpha contains the stage limit J. What is proved, and what the bound needs, is that one bound holds at every stage of a trial, so denominators do not compound from stage to stage.
findings.evidence: In appendix-growth.tex:119, alpha = J + max_i|e_i| + |E| + mu K_mu. A node is a center plus or minus 2^{E-j-e_i}((2^mu+1)^k - 2^{mu k})/2^{mu(k-1)}, and the numerator is odd. So the 2-adic denominator exponent is up to J + |E| + max|e_i| + mu K_mu, which grows linearly with J. The bound is uniform over the stages j <= J because centers and clipped endpoints are earlier nodes.
findings.fix: growth.tex: replace 'so they do not grow with the number of stages' with 'so one bound holds at all stages of a trial: denominators do not compound from stage to stage'. appendix-growth.tex:129: replace 'So denominators do not grow with the number of stages.' with 'So the bound does not compound from stage to stage; it depends on the stage limit only through the term J in alpha.'

Exact-arithmetic checks (new scripts in process/w4/checks/) confirm all formulas of Proposition 7.5(A),(B), Examples C.2 and C.9, Proposition 7.13 and the ladder C.10. On random instances they also confirm the cut identity, the threshold-encoded minimum cut, CORE's invariants (b)-(d), the height bound of Lemma D.1, the exact-output pipeline of Theorem D.2 and the submodularity in D.3(c). What remains is five minor problems. Three sentences overstate what is proved: the Section 7.2 title, a remark in 7.1, and the comparison in Theorem 7.10(iv), which holds only for the Euclidean kappa. The other two: Theorem 7.10(iii) does not say that its exact procedure may not stop without growth, and a robustness sentence in Theorem 7.17 is imprecise. findings.issue: Theorem 7.10(iv) says 'the parameter never exceeds the one obtained by keeping the private variables as ordinary coordinates'. The proof compares only the Euclidean numbers kappa(L^+,g_V) and kappa(L_F,g_F). The approximation theorem for the problem with the private variables kept (Thm 5.9(b)) uses the weighted kappa-bar, which can be much smaller. Theorems 7.2(b) and 7.10(iii) are stated only with the Euclidean kappa_V.
findings.evidence: Take r=0 (or a block that does not couple) and F_0(v)=100 v_1^2+v_2^2 on [-1,1]^2. Then L^+=200, g=1, kappa_V=200, so Thm 7.10(iii) gives f(p,200)200^C(I+q+1)^C. But F=(1/2)(200v_1^2+2v_2^2) has weighted growth with gamma=1/2, so kappa-bar=2, and Thm 5.9(b) gives f(p,2)(I+q+1)^5. The stronger statement is true. If F-OPT >= gamma sum L_i^F (x_i-x_i^*)^2 and L_i^+ <= max{(H_0)_ii,0}=L_i^F, then V(v)-OPT=F(v,y(v))-OPT >= gamma sum_{i in K} L_i^+ (v_i-v_i^*)^2, so kappa-bar_V <= kappa-bar_F. App. C.1(b) already uses only weighted growth of V.
findings.fix: Replace the second sentence of (iv) with: 'Thus kappa(L^+,g) never exceeds the Euclidean condition number kappa(L,g) of F with the private variables kept as ordinary coordinates.' Optional strengthening: state Thm 7.2(b) and Thm 7.10(iii) under weighted growth of V with kappa-bar_V, and add to (iv): 'and V inherits weighted growth from F with kappa-bar_V <= kappa-bar_F, because L_i^+ <= L_i^F.'

findings.issue: The exact procedure of Theorem 7.10(iii) has no termination guarantee without point growth, and the text does not say so. Theorem 6.14 (EX) and Theorem 7.2(c) do stop on every instance, and the results table lists Theorem 7.10 next to them, so a reader may assume the same here.
findings.evidence: The procedure rounds each continuous retained coordinate of the incumbent to a rational with denominator at most Lambda_0. Without uniqueness, the incumbents may approach a continuum of minimizers whose points have larger denominators, so the acceptance test may never pass. REC is not available because the slices are polytopes (w3 F67). The theorem itself claims a bound only under growth and validity without growth, so no stated claim is false.

verdict: Every reduction and lower bound in Section 10 and Appendix G is correct as stated, and none of the five findings below changes a result. I re-derived each proof and tested every construction on small instances in exact arithmetic (four scripts in process/w4/checks/, all PASS, plus a negative control). This covers Prop 10.1 with Cor 10.2, Remarks G.1 and 10.4, Props 10.3 and 10.5–10.10, Lemma G.2, Props G.3 and G.5, and Remark G.6. The issues from rounds w2/w3 are fixed: the set-growth scope, the t_c argument, the rETH attribution and definition, the Clique to multicolored-clique step, effective o(p), occupied widths, the alpha decoding and the L=0 instance. I checked Remark G.1 against the Del Pia–Khajavirad source (Theorem 3, eqs. (18)–(24), Remark 2) and the Bienstock–Muñoz attribution against their Appendix A. All five findings are minor: (1) the summaries of the rETH result omit that the polynomial in I has fixed degree, which matters because kappa and I are polynomially related on the hard instances; (2) the comparison after the oracle barrier does not separate it from CT, which also needs more queries at higher accuracy, only logarithmically; (3) SETH is used without being defined; (4) the remark on the Del Pia–Khajavirad reduction says "exponential in the input length" when the input length is Theta(k log k); (5) the Bienstock–Muñoz citation lacks its locator. The full report is at /workspace/minlp-notes/paper-decomposition-aware/process/w4/M-limits.md.

\paragraph{Conditional recourse.} The condition number is built from diagonal curvature, so a stiff convex term inflates it even when the subproblem it defines is easy. We therefore also allow \emph{recourse}: exact minimization over some variables $y$ for fixed values $v$ of the others. Partial minimization over a box preserves upper coordinate curvatures and growth, so the certificate and the growth analysis apply to the value function $V(v)=\min_yF(v,y)$ whenever $V$ can be evaluated exactly (Theorem~\ref{thm:valuefn}). For private convex quadratic blocks, the optimal responses are piecewise affine and certify a reduction of the coordinate curvatures of $V$ that is the largest possible for the block (Theorem~\ref{thm:cv} and Proposition~\ref{prop:vf-curv}). If a quadratic $F$ is concave in each recourse variable and submodular in them after sign changes, each recourse problem is one minimum cut with a flow certificate, so only the remaining variables are gridded (Theorems~\ref{thm:cr-oracle} and~\ref{thm:cr-search}). For balanced box quadratics the grid problem itself is a minimum cut, so no tree decomposition is needed: under point growth, certified approximation takes $(n\kappa(I+q+1))^{O(1)}$ bit operations (Theorem~\ref{thm:balanced}). Recourse does not reduce the parameter to the ratio of negative curvature to growth in general (Proposition~\ref{prop:cv-limit}). Parametric quadratic programming, cut representations of submodular quadratic functions and threshold encodings of ordered labels are classical; what is new is the curvature and growth accounting that keeps them inside the certificate.

verdict.reasoning:
The finding is real. I checked it against the paper, the W3 history and the local full text of Hochbaum-Shanthikumar (HS) at /workspace/minlp-notes/literature/papers/hochbaum1990-convex-separable-optimization-is-not/fulltext.md. The check script is /workspace/minlp-notes/paper-decomposition-aware/process/w4/checks/verify-C-literature-1.py; it was run once and every check passed.

1. **HS is cited once and described too narrowly.** HochbaumShanthikumar1990 appears only at related.tex:115, as an algorithm "logarithmic in the domain size for linear and separable convex integer programs". HS also covers the continuous case:
   - Sec. 1.3 says the box is halved each iteration, there are log2(B/2eps) iterations for the continuous problem, and "the interval for each variable is divided into a grid of O(n Delta) points".
   - Thm 1.1 gives log2(B/2eps) T(8n^2 Delta, m, Delta).
   - Alg. 4.3 / Thm 4.4 is the continuous algorithm. Each iteration grids a window of width 4n s_{k-1} Delta around the previous solution with a factor 8n Delta. Proximity comes from Thms 3.7 and 3.8.
   - Alg. 4.2 / Thm 4.3 is the totally unimodular (TU) case, where each scaled integer problem is one linear program (LP).

   This is the same template as CT and especially TU-GRID: grids of fixed size per stage, a halving mesh h_j = eta 2^{-j}, a region of radius O(sqrt(n_c kappa_c) h_j) (Thm thm:tu-states, a_j + h_j), and O(log(1/eps)) stages.

2. **The comparison was deleted and never relocated.** The pre-W3 rem:tu-bm contained a correct HS paragraph (process/w3/sections-before-w3/constraints.tex:840-847). The tu agent deleted it (reports/tu.md:49) and proposed an optional sentence for related.tex (tu.md:139-145), which was never added. A grep of all sections finds no other mention of proximity scaling or HS, so nothing else in the paper covers it.

3. **Meyer (1977) is a real omission.** Its Crossref metadata matches the reviewer's BibTeX, and the abstract reads: "separable convex objective function and a totally unimodular constraint matrix ... solve the problem by a single, easily-constructed linear program". It rests on the same integrality as lem:tu-round (Hoffman-Kruskal on a cell polytope with aligned data). related.tex:204-207 credits only Hoffman-Kruskal and dependent rounding.

**Where the reviewer is wrong or imprecise:**
- **(a) related.tex:141-143 needs no change.** "None of these methods" is scoped to the adaptive-discretization paragraph, and HS does not certify anyway, so even a field-wide reading is not falsified by HS.
- **(b) The proposed text misstates HS's accuracy.** HS's "eps-accurate" means a point within eps of an optimal solution in the sup-norm (HS p. 858). It is not an objective gap, and the paper's accuracy is a certified objective gap. "Accuracy eps" alone would mislead.
- **(c) The locator "Theorems 1.1 and 3.3" is wrong for the continuous algorithm.** Thm 3.3 is the integer-versus-continuous proximity result. The continuous algorithm uses Thms 3.8 and 4.4.
- **(d) "The window comes from growth instead of proximity" is imprecise for this paper.** The retained region is chosen by min-marginal filtering, which needs no assumption and yields the certificate. Growth only bounds its size.

**Severity.** This is a literature-positioning gap, not a mathematical error. It is major because HS is the closest classical antecedent of the stage-wise, accuracy-independent grids, and of TU-GRID in particular. An integer-programming referee would very likely ask for the comparison. The fix is small and local, and it respects the "one place per comparison" convention.

The scaling algorithm of Hochbaum and Shanthikumar is the closest classical analogue of our stages. For a separable convex objective over $\{x:Ax\ge b\}$, each iteration minimizes a piecewise-linear interpolation of the objective on a grid of $O(n\Delta)$ points per variable, where $\Delta$ bounds the subdeterminants of $A$. The grid lies in a box around the previous solution, and a proximity theorem allows the box to be halved. The proximity theorem guarantees this accuracy, but the algorithm does not produce a certificate of it. Here the objective is nonseparable and nonconvex. The retained region is chosen by min-marginal filtering, which needs no assumption and yields a certificate, and growth only bounds its size. verdict.reasoning:
The finding is correct, and I could not refute it.

The code. experiments/run_all.py task_scip, lines about 262-280, clips SCIP's point with `v = min(max(v, lo), hi)` before `exact_val = problem.value(...)`. So `exact_value_of_scip_point`, `exact_gap`, `scip_point_excess_over_fstar` (the 1.3e-14) and `epigraph_shortfall` all describe the point after projection onto the box. The paper never mentions this projection; grep finds no "clip" or "project" in sections/computation.tex. The text at computation.tex:368-375 ("Its incumbents were optimal to within 1.3e-14 ... because the epigraph constraint is satisfied only within a feasibility tolerance") and the Table 5 caption (394-398) describe these numbers as properties of SCIP's own incumbent.

The mathematics. In planted() the gradient at x* is ell, with ell_i = -mu x*_i on the active set A. Moving an active coordinate outward by delta therefore lowers F by mu*delta to first order. The free coordinates move only by about 1e-8, so their effect is second order.

Independent check. I wrote process/w4/checks/verify-C-computation-1.py and ran it as one process. It rebuilds the E5 model exactly as task_scip does. The primal and dual bounds matched E5_scip.csv to all printed digits on path16 s202, band2-12 s101, tree16 s303, band3-8 s303 and path32 s101. In each run:
- The violated coordinates are exactly the planted active set A (4, 3, 4, 2 and 8 coordinates), each violated outward by 9.9996e-9.
- SCIP's own checkSol(original, checkbounds=True) reports the solution as feasible.
- F at the clipped point is about 1e-15, and the exact split of the shortfall is: path16 s202, 1.820e-6 = 0.920e-6 (bounds) + 0.900e-6 (epigraph); band12 s101, 3.045e-6 = 2.145e-6 + 0.900e-6; path32 s101, 3.580e-6 = 2.680e-6 + 0.900e-6.
- The bound part equals mu*sum(violations) to all printed digits.

A fit to all 21 CSV rows of shortfall = n_A*mu*1e-8 + 9e-7 holds with relative error at most 3e-4. The bound share runs from 0.5055 (path16 s202) to 0.9441 (path128 s101), as the reviewer said. The reviewer's logs for path128 s101 (32 coordinates) and path32 with feastol 1e-9 agree with this.

Consequences. SCIP's actual incumbents are infeasible by about 1e-8, which is within tolerance. Their exact objective lies below OPT by n_A*mu*1e-8, between 0.92e-6 and 1.5e-5, so the sentence "Its incumbents were optimal to within 1.3e-14" is false as written. The stated cause of the shortfall is mostly wrong: the epigraph violation accounts for only 6% to 49% of it.

What still holds. The gap numbers (2.8e-6 to 6.8e-6), the validity of the dual bounds, the shortfall range (1.8e-6 to 1.6e-5) and the conclusion that SCIP's interval never contains OPT are all unaffected. Projection is also the right choice for a valid upper bound.

Severity. No theorem and no headline conclusion changes, and the conclusion's general sentence ("solvers satisfy constraints only within tolerances") stays true. Still, the paper states a false empirical fact and a wrong mechanism, and a reader who evaluates SCIP's incumbent would see the contradiction at once. I rate it major for correctness of reported results, but low-impact.

The corrected fix below avoids $\mu$ and gives the measured violation as "about $10^{-8}$" (measured: 9.9996e-9).
